newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Holocaust fund starts work, eyes fast payout.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Holocaust fund starts work, eyes fast payout.

text.p: The executive committee of Switzerland's Holocaust memorial fund got down to business on Monday and pledged to start distributing money as quickly as possible to the Nazis' needy victims and their families.

With the clock inexorably ticking for Holocaust survivors, now averaging 80 years old, there is no time to lose in handing out millions of dollars in humanitarian aid donated by Swiss banks and private businesses, panel members said.

"We want to discuss today a fast-track process to be able to make the first payments as quickly as possible but still in a controlled manner," Chairman Rolf Bloch, also head of the Swiss Jewish Federation, told reporters before the seven-member panel began its first meeting.
"The issue is not opening an office, but providing aid quickly."

He did not say which groups might get part of the 160 million Swiss francs ($109.4 million) in donations already paid in by private businesses eager to bolster Switzerland's image amid foreign criticism that it cynically profited from World War Two.

Panel members have cited the special plight of Holocaust survivors in eastern Europe, known as "double victims" for their inbility to get compensation during the Cold War for their suffering during Hitler's systematic murder of six million Jews and many others deemed unworthy to live.

The Swiss central bank, which admits it bought gold from Nazi Germany that it should have known was looted from the countries and peoples overrun by Hitler's troops, also plans to contribute 100 million francs if parliament approves.
Bloch said he and his colleagues -- three representatives of Jewish groups and three Swiss -- wanted to press ahead even though the fund's secretariat had not yet been formed.
Today's meeting would focus on finding consensus for priorities and ground rules for distributing funds to worthy groups and projects rather than individuals.

"This would allow us to release a certain part of the fund's money as early as today for processing in line with proposals from the advisory council and from organisations that guarantee that funds are used in a correct and supervisable way," he said.
World Jewish Congress (WJC) secretary general Israel Singer, sitting in for WJC President Edgar Bronfman, hailed the panel's no-nonsense approach.
"The efforts that we make here today will augur well for the beginning of a new environment, we hope, between the Jewish people and Switzerland and between the world and Switzerland," he said.
"This will create good public relations because the only good public relations in the world is good public conduct. That is what we are doing here today," he said.

Singer was referring to months of wrangling between Swiss banks and Jewish groups over accusations that banks are hoarding billions of dollars in dormant wealth of Holocaust victims, a charge the financial institutions deny.
Bloch said as many as a million people could qualify for help from the fund, which he stressed was humanitarian and would not address individuals' claims against Switzerland.

"We would be very happy if we are able today to set something in motion with this fast-track process even if we know that we will never be able -- neither today nor in the future -- to help all the needy as much as we would like."

The fund is separate from the Swiss government's plan to create a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian fund that would use sales of official gold reserves to help victims of poverty, disasters and human rights abuses.
